title: Femoral embolectomy
subtitle: Balloon catheter embolectomy for acute limb ischaemia

sources.title: ESVS 2020 Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Management of Acute Limb Ischaemia

sources.org: Fogarty TJ et al., Surgery, Gynecology and Obstetrics
sources.title: A method for extraction of arterial emboli and thrombi

indications: Acute embolic occlusion of the common femoral, iliac or femoropopliteal arteries with a threatened limb (Rutherford IIa or IIb).
Saddle embolus of the aortic bifurcation, through bilateral groin incisions.
Thrombosis where an initial embolectomy will be combined with on-table angiography and further revascularisation.
contraindications: Irreversible ischaemia (Rutherford III), where revascularisation risks fatal reperfusion injury.
A limb that can wait and has thrombosis on extensive chronic disease, which may be better served by imaging and a planned procedure.
preparation: Heparin given at diagnosis; potassium, CK, renal function and group and save checked.
Local anaesthesia with anaesthetic monitoring is suitable for many patients; general anaesthesia for an uncooperative patient or when a bypass or fasciotomy is likely.
Fluoroscopy and contrast available for on-table angiography.
Consent for fasciotomy, further bypass and, rarely, amputation.
positioning: Supine, with the whole affected leg prepped and free, and the other groin prepped for access or vein harvest.
equipment: Balloon embolectomy catheters in several sizes, typically 3 to 5 French for the leg.
Vascular tray, slings, bulldog clamps and fine monofilament sutures; patch material.
anatomy: The common femoral artery lies at the mid-inguinal point, midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis, lateral to the femoral vein.
It divides into the superficial femoral and profunda femoris arteries a few centimetres below the inguinal ligament; the bifurcation is where emboli lodge.
The femoral nerve lies lateral to the artery, outside the femoral sheath.
The circumflex iliac and inferior epigastric vessels arise near the inguinal ligament and bleed if not controlled.
criticalSafety: Inflate the balloon only enough to feel gentle contact with the wall as it is withdrawn. Over-inflation causes intimal injury, dissection and rupture.
Pass the catheter into the profunda as well as the superficial femoral artery; the profunda may save the limb.
Completion imaging before closing. Clinical signs on the table are unreliable.
Decide on fasciotomy before leaving theatre.
structuresAtRisk: Popliteal and tibial arteries during catheter passage
commonErrors: Delaying theatre for CT in a IIb limb with a clear embolic history.
Accepting poor back-bleeding without on-table angiography.
Over-inflating the balloon and creating a dissection.
Closing a longitudinal arteriotomy primarily in a small artery, narrowing it.
complications: Reperfusion injury: hyperkalaemia, acidosis, myoglobinuria and renal failure.
Arterial injury from the catheter: dissection, perforation, arteriovenous fistula.
Groin haematoma, lymphocele and wound infection.
Death, reflecting the patient's cardiac disease.
postop: Hourly limb observations, compartment checks and urine output for the first day.
Continue heparin and convert to long-term anticoagulation for an embolic source unless contraindicated.
Echocardiography and cardiology review for the source; send the embolus for histology.

steps.emphasis: Include fasciotomy, bypass, amputation and death. These are frail patients with cardiac disease.
The whole limb must be visible and accessible, so that the foot can be examined under the drapes.
Prepare the whole affected leg circumferentially to the toes, in a clear bag, and the contralateral groin and leg for vein or access.
Sling the common femoral, superficial femoral and profunda femoris arteries separately.
Usually already given at diagnosis. Top it up per local protocol before clamping.
On-table angiography is routine after embolectomy, not an optional extra.
Send the embolus for histology: an atrial myxoma or tumour embolus changes the whole management.

step.emb.groin-exposure.title: Exposure of the femoral bifurcation
step.emb.groin-exposure.why: The common femoral bifurcation gives access to the iliac, superficial femoral and profunda arteries through one incision, and is where emboli most often lodge.
how: Make a vertical incision over the femoral artery, from just above the inguinal ligament downwards, centred on the mid-inguinal point.
Divide the femoral sheath over the artery, ligating lymphatics to reduce lymphocele.
Expose the common femoral artery and its bifurcation, identifying the profunda origin posterolaterally.
pitfalls: An incision too low, which finds the superficial femoral artery and misses the profunda.

step.emb.arteriotomy.title: Arteriotomy
step.emb.arteriotomy.why: The site and direction of the arteriotomy decide how easily the catheter enters each branch and whether the artery can be closed without narrowing.
how: A transverse arteriotomy in the common femoral artery just above the bifurcation in a soft, healthy artery: it closes primarily without narrowing.
A longitudinal arteriotomy if the artery is diseased and an endarterectomy, patch or bypass may follow.
Remove any embolus visible at the arteriotomy before passing catheters.
pitfalls: Cutting the back wall with the knife.
A transverse arteriotomy in a heavily diseased artery that then cannot be extended.

step.emb.catheter-passes.title: Balloon catheter passes
step.emb.catheter-passes.why: The balloon catheter extracts clot from vessels that cannot be reached directly. The technique is simple; the harm comes from force and from stopping before the job is done.
how: Pass an appropriately sized catheter proximally into the iliac system until inflow is pulsatile and strong.
Pass catheters distally into the superficial femoral and profunda arteries, as far as they go, inflating the balloon gently while withdrawing, with the operator feeling the wall.
Repeat until two consecutive passes return no clot and back-bleeding is brisk.
If catheters will not pass beyond the knee or back-bleeding stays poor, proceed to on-table angiography and consider a separate below-knee popliteal exploration.
structuresAtRisk: Intima of the superficial femoral and popliteal arteries
pitfalls: Over-inflating the balloon, causing intimal damage that later thromboses.

step.emb.arteriotomy-closure.title: Closure of the arteriotomy
step.emb.arteriotomy-closure.why: A closure that narrows the artery creates the stenosis that will thrombose the repair.
how: Close a transverse arteriotomy primarily with interrupted or continuous fine monofilament sutures.
Close a longitudinal arteriotomy with a patch (vein or prosthetic) unless the artery is large.
Flush and back-bleed before tying the final suture.
pitfalls: Primary closure of a longitudinal arteriotomy in a small artery.
Raising an intimal flap with the needle on the distal edge.

step.emb.fasciotomy-decision.title: Fasciotomy decision
step.emb.fasciotomy-decision.why: Reperfusion swelling causes compartment syndrome hours later, often at night, when nerve and muscle loss are then irreversible. The decision is cheapest in theatre.
how: Consider four-compartment fasciotomy after prolonged ischaemia, after a IIb limb, or when the calf is already tense.
Use two incisions, lateral and medial, decompressing all four compartments.
If not done, document the reasoning and arrange regular compartment checks.
pitfalls: Deferring the decision to the ward team overnight.
A single incision that misses the deep posterior compartment.
